title: Waves
line: The primes are made of waves
summary: What the hypothesis says, where the zeros show up in a count of primes, and how the proof turns “nothing to the right of the line” into “everything on it”.
story: The goal is fixed first. `Statements.lean` writes the hypotheses in Mathlib’s own terms, and `Main.lean` derives all five headline theorems from a single result, `grh`: no Dirichlet L-function vanishes to the right of the line Re s = 1/2.

The step from “nothing to the right” to “everything on the line” is the mirror symmetry of zeros (`New/Main`, `Lib/Analytic/ZeroSymmetry`). A zero off the line would have a twin on the other side, and one of the two would sit to the right.

The waves enter through a weighted count of primes. `PrimeError` defines its remainder R_q. Its transform has poles exactly at zeros of L-functions, so each zero contributes a wave to the count. `PrimeNumberTheorem` shows that R_q tends to 0, which the proof uses at a far-out second cut-off.

title: A ceiling
line: A bound from above is enough
summary: An upper bound on the prime remainder, never a lower one, rules out zeros to the right of the line. The main inequality supplies it.
story: `Zeros/Criterion` is the key reduction. An eventual bound from above, R_q(x) ≤ A·x^(β−1), excludes zeros to the right of β. No floor is needed. Its notes trace the idea to Landau (1905) and recent work of Suzuki.

`OneSidedBound` proves that ceiling with exponent −1/2 + ε, which is exactly what the line Re s = 1/2 demands, and ends with `grh`. The GUIDE says the ε comes from log⁶ b / m, so the number of lifts m does the work.

Where does the ceiling come from? `MainInequality` measures one lattice of modular forms in two ways: from above (Theorems A and B, chapter 4) and from below (Theorem C, the bill). A “main amount” appears on both sides and cancels. What is left bounds the prime remainder from above. `Data`, `PrimeSums` and `Lattices` set up the scales, the prime sums and the heights and covolumes being compared.

title: Multiplicity
summary: A nonzero number can’t have more prime factors than its size. Derivatives of theta functions give numbers whose divisibility by primes is guaranteed.
story: This is the whole-number version of Stepanov’s 1969 trick. A polynomial can’t have more roots, counted with multiplicity, than its degree. Likewise, a nonzero whole number can’t carry more prime factors, weighted by log p, than its own size. Guaranteed divisibility therefore becomes an upper bound on a sum over primes.

The numbers come from derivatives. A “jet” is a Taylor coefficient P(∂)F(0) of a theta function. `Derivatives/Divisibility` shows these derivatives are divisible by primes in a controlled way: the GUIDE calls them “derivatives that count primes”. `Field`, `FormalGroup` and `Vacuum` set up the algebra, and `Sharpness` shows the bound is attained.
The payoff is the gain: how many times each prime must divide the composite lift of chapter 4. Each extra layer of guaranteed divisibility plays the part of extra multiplicity.

title: The chain
line: A chain of about √x theta lifts
summary: Each lift adds a layer of divisibility. The chain’s length, between √x and 2√x lifts, balances cost against error at the square root.
story: The GUIDE’s size table fixes the number of lifts m between √x and 2√x. That is the square root Alpöge singles out in his note: he says Claude suggested the chain’s length.

`UpperBound` builds the chain. Source forms are lifted m times between definite hermitian spaces X₀ → X_m and restricted to Y_m: the composite lift. The seesaw identity (`Seesaw/SeesawIdentity`) says that the lower chain applied to Poincaré series is a constant times this composite lift. `UpperBound/Divisibility` and `UpperBound/Size` then show the lifts are highly divisible and not too big.

That gives Theorem A (`Reduction/ShortAndEnough`): a multiple of the projected Poincaré series has short lifts and small index. `Spanning` proves Theorem B with a second-moment argument (Bessel functions, unfolding): a few translates span almost all of the target forms. Together they are the upper half of the main inequality.

title: Paying for the lifts
line: The lower bound, where most of the code lives
summary: Theorem C: the lattice can’t be too small. This is where Galois representations, Selmer groups and L-values come in.
story: Every lift has a price. Theorem C (`Determinant/Twist/LongForms`) is the lower half of the main inequality: covolume and twice the index together are at least about the main amount. Proving it is where most of the code lives.

`Determinant` chooses a twist for each prime, computes norms of theta lifts and of whole chains, and uses an exchange identity of Siegel–Weil type. `OneLift` studies a single lift: its volume and height, Hecke L-values as squared norms and their valuations, and “false lifts”.

`Congruences` controls the denominators. It uses Galois representations, anticyclotomic twists with small Selmer groups, the local loss, and the lifting of crystalline classes (p-adic Hodge theory). `Appendix` supplies discrete series with a large gap. This is the “everything” behind the remark that “the Riemann Hypothesis is proved by using everything”.
